newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: IMF mission to start talks on new loan to Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: IMF mission to start talks on new loan to Pakistan.

text.p: An International Monetary Fund mission is due to start talks on a new medium-term loan to Pakistan this week, an IMF official said on Monday.
The mission, led by Antonio Furtado, division chief of the IMF's Middle Eastern department, will stay in Islamabad until the end July. World Bank representatives will take part.
The team will initiate discussions on a new ESAF (Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility), IMF resident representative Shamsuddin Tareq told Reuters. He gave no other details.

The team will review Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz's budget for fiscal 1997/98 (July-June) and discuss the government's structural reform plans as part of efforts to reach agreement on a new ESAF to tide Pakistan through its economic difficulties.
The cash-strapped government wants the IMF, which scrapped a standby loan to Pakistan in March, to agree an ESAF loan by September, but analysts said such swift action was unlikely.
"This team is here to review the post-budget scene and will make no comment before reporting to the IMF board," said Mudassar Malik, chief dealer at BMA Capital Management in Karachi.
"The government is keen that the IMF should give an early statement to dispel doubts about the state of the economy."
He said the IMF was unlikely to start disbursing a new loan before September or October. Other analysts said the ESAF, if it went ahead, might not be available until November.
A key part of the IMF mission's task will be to assess whether the budget can actually deliver the non-negotiable IMF target of a deficit of five percent of gross domestic product.
Aziz vowed on budget day to curb spending to cut the deficit to five percent of GDP from 6.2 percent in 1996/97 and to focus on reviving economic growth through tax and tariff cuts.
"These are our four critical targets: seven percent industrial growth, five percent agricultural growth, six percent GDP growth and 15 percent export growth," he said.
In 1996/97 manufacturing grew an estimated 1.8 percent, agriculture 0.7 percent and gross domestic product 3.1 percent, while exports expanded 1.1 percent in the first nine months.
The IMF mission is likely to look at last year's outcome, for which some figures have yet to be completed, and scrutinise the budget to ensure any new ESAF sits on a realistic base.
They will look at the revenue impact of the budget measures, one analyst said, adding if there is any softness in the projections, there will have to be new measures to make it up.
Raza Mirza, chief analyst at KASB Co, said no early breakthrough should be expected from the IMF visit.
Pakistan has major debt servicing payments from September to November, he said. at the same time the government should push on with its policies for structural reforms.
Analysts said the IMF and the government seemed in broad agreement on the type of structural reforms needed, but their speed and timing would need detailed negotiation.

Pakistan signed a $1.5 billion, three-year ESAF lending programme with the IMF in February 1994, but the IMF halted disbursements after the former government led by Benazir Bhutto announced a 1995/96 budget that failed to meet agreed targets.
A balance of payments crisis in October 1995 forced the Bhutto government to seek an IMF standby loan, which was suspended in March last year, again because of missed targets.

The standby was resumed and expanded in December after a caretaker government took over from the dismissed Bhutto, but the IMF again halted it in March when Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government said the targets were out of reach.
At that time the IMF welcomed Sharif's plans for structural reform, including tax reform and tax administration reform, faster privatisation, and revival of industry and farming.

The government's policy package, when implemented fully, will lay the basis for a transition to negotiations of a medium-term ESAF/EFF arrangement, it said. These could start immediately after successful implementation of these policies.
Analysts said the ESAF was likely to go through, but some questioned whether it would be a mere sticking plaster, or enough to pull pakistan's economy out of its downhill slide.
There is no sign yet that the economy is starting to pickup, one analyst said.
The government's whole strategy depends on industrial revival to generate more tax revenue.
"We need to establish confidence in the economy and see local and foreign investment flowing in," he added.
